explain.say: In March 1946, in a small college town in Missouri, Winston Churchill warned that an iron curtain had come down across Europe, from the Baltic to the Adriatic. Just a year earlier Britain, America and the Soviet Union had been allies. Look at the timeline. How did friends become rivals so quickly?

explain.say: See the causes. Two rival systems: American capitalist democracy and Soviet one-party communism. Stalin, whose country had lost about 27 million people, wanted friendly governments as a buffer. The Americans feared communism would spread. Each side's defence looked like attack to the other. Which cause feels most like misunderstanding?

draw.name: x-why
draw.question: Why did wartime allies become enemies?

because.label: Fate of Germany
because.note: Rebuild it or keep it weak?

because.label: Mutual fear
because.note: Each saw the other's defence as attack.

draw.answer: Different systems, real interests and mutual fear.

explain.say: Now the map. At Yalta and Potsdam the Big Three split Germany and Berlin into four zones. By 1948 communist governments ruled Poland, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia. In 1947 President Truman promised to help free peoples resist pressure: containment, meaning stopping communism spreading. Why would Berlin, deep in the Soviet zone, become a flashpoint?

Look at the sizes. Through the Marshall Plan, the United States gave about 13 billion dollars from 1948 to 1952 to rebuild Western Europe; Britain got about 3.3 billion, France about 2.3. Stalin refused it for the East. Then in June 1948 he blockaded West Berlin, and the West flew in supplies for almost a year. Was aid generosity, strategy, or both?

Now the debate. Orthodox historians blamed Soviet expansion; revisionists like William Appleman Williams blamed American economic ambition; post-revisionists like John Lewis Gaddis saw fear and misreading on both sides. Great work. Exam tip: name the school, then test it on one event, like the Berlin Blockade.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Post-revisionists: fear and misreading on both sides.

faq.a: Rival ideologies, disputes over Eastern Europe and Germany, Soviet security fears after a devastating war, American fears of communist expansion, the atomic bomb and mutual mistrust turned wartime allies into rivals between 1945 and 1949.

The European Recovery Program, proposed by US Secretary of State George Marshall in June 1947, which gave about 13 billion dollars in aid to Western Europe from 1948 to 1952. The Soviet Union refused it and kept Eastern Europe out.
asks: How much was the Marshall Plan worth?

faq.q: Who was to blame for the Cold War?
faq.a: Orthodox historians blamed Stalin's expansion; revisionists such as William Appleman Williams and Gabriel Kolko blamed American economic and atomic power; post-revisionists such as John Lewis Gaddis stressed mutual fear and misperception. Soviet archives opened after 1991 have fed the debate.
asks: What is the revisionist view of the Cold War?

faq.a: Winston Churchill's image, in a speech at Fulton, Missouri, on 5 March 1946, for the line dividing Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe from the West.
asks: Where did Churchill give the iron curtain speech?

faq.a: From June 1948 to May 1949 the Soviet Union cut road, rail and canal routes to West Berlin. The Western powers supplied the city by air, the Berlin Airlift, until Stalin lifted the blockade.

facts: Churchill gave his iron curtain speech on 5 March 1946.
The Berlin Blockade lasted from June 1948 to May 1949.

quiz.say: Britain received about 3.3 and France about 2.3 billion dollars of Marshall aid. How much more did Britain get?

wrong.1: 5.6 billion is the two amounts added together.

quiz.say: What was the aim of containment?
quiz.why: Containment aimed to stop further communist expansion without direct war with the USSR.

wrong.1: The USA did not plan to invade the Soviet Union.
wrong.2: The USA kept its atomic secrets, which fed Soviet suspicion.
